excerpts.location: OF THE MENSURATION OF THE CIRCLE
excerpts.latex: A magnitude or ratio, which is fixed in value by the conditions of the question, is called a \Emph{Constant}.
excerpts.markdown: A magnitude or ratio, which is fixed in value by the conditions of the question, is called a Constant.
excerpts.why: Gives the learner a plain definition of a constant before any limit argument.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.location: OF THE MENSURATION OF THE CIRCLE
excerpts.latex: If two variables are at every instant equal their limits are equal.
excerpts.markdown: If two variables are at every instant equal their limits are equal.
excerpts.why: States the lemma that the whole chapter's limit arguments rest on, in one sentence a learner can hold.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.location: OF THE MENSURATION OF THE CIRCLE
excerpts.latex: Then if the number of sides of the polygons increase these two ratios vary but remain always equal to each other, therefore (Lemma) their limits are equal.
excerpts.markdown: Then if the number of sides of the polygons increase these two ratios vary but remain always equal to each other, therefore (Lemma) their limits are equal.
excerpts.why: Shows the limiting argument in action: two ratios that stay equal must share a limit.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.location: OF THE MENSURATION OF THE CIRCLE
excerpts.latex: The area of any circular sector is half the rectangle contained by its arc and the radius of the circle.
excerpts.markdown: The area of any circular sector is half the rectangle contained by its arc and the radius of the circle.
excerpts.why: A memorable statement of the sector area rule that a learner can check against a simple circle.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.location: OF THE MENSURATION OF THE CIRCLE
excerpts.latex: Let a number of points be taken in a terminated curve line, and let straight lines be drawn from each point to the next, then if the number of points be conceived to increase and the distance between each two to diminish continually, the extremities remaining fixed, the limit of the sum of the straight lines is called the \Emph{Length of the Curve}.
excerpts.markdown: Let a number of points be taken in a terminated curve line, and let straight lines be drawn from each point to the next, then if the number of points be conceived to increase and the distance between each two to diminish continually, the extremities remaining fixed, the limit of the sum of the straight lines is called the Length of the Curve.
excerpts.why: Defines arc length by a limit of inscribed polygonal lines, the idea a learner needs for curved lengths.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.location: OF THE MENSURATION OF THE CIRCLE
excerpts.latex: By the method of ``continued fractions'' it will be found that $\dfrac{22}{7}$~and~$\dfrac{355}{113}$ are nearer approximations to the value of~$\pi$ than any simpler fractions.
excerpts.markdown: By the method of “continued fractions” it will be found that $\dfrac{22}{7}$ and $\dfrac{355}{113}$ are nearer approximations to the value of $\pi$ than any simpler fractions.
excerpts.why: Gives learners a concrete sense of how close simple fractions come to pi.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.location: OF THE MENSURATION OF THE CIRCLE
excerpts.latex: Of these $\dfrac{22}{7}$ ($=3.14$) is the approximation discovered by Archimedes (killed, it is said, at the siege of Syracuse,
excerpts.markdown: Of these $\dfrac{22}{7}$ ($=3.14$) is the approximation discovered by Archimedes (killed, it is said, at the siege of Syracuse,
excerpts.why: A historical remark placing the 22/7 approximation with Archimedes.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.location: OF THE AREA OF A TRIANGLE AND OF THE INSCRIBED CIRCLE
excerpts.latex: A triangle is equal to the rectangle contained by its semi-perimeter and the radius of the inscribed circle.
excerpts.markdown: A triangle is equal to the rectangle contained by its semi-perimeter and the radius of the inscribed circle.
excerpts.why: States the chapter's first result in one line, so a learner sees the area formula in terms of half the perimeter and the inscribed radius.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.location: OF THE AREA OF A TRIANGLE AND OF THE INSCRIBED CIRCLE
excerpts.latex: The two tangents from each angle to the inscribed circle are equal: hence, if three tangents, one from each angle, be taken, their sum is the semi-perimeter, and therefore a tangent from one of the angles, together with the side opposite that angle, is equal to the semi-perimeter.
excerpts.markdown: The two tangents from each angle to the inscribed circle are equal: hence, if three tangents, one from each angle, be taken, their sum is the semi-perimeter, and therefore a tangent from one of the angles, together with the side opposite that angle, is equal to the semi-perimeter.
excerpts.why: Shows why a tangent plus the opposite side equals the semi-perimeter, a short argument a learner can follow step by step.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.location: OF THE AREA OF A TRIANGLE AND OF THE INSCRIBED CIRCLE
excerpts.latex: Let two of the sides of the triangle $ABC$ be produced, and a circle described touching the two produced sides and the third side.
excerpts.markdown: Let two of the sides of the triangle $ABC$ be produced, and a circle described touching the two produced sides and the third side.
excerpts.why: Defines the excircle by construction, giving the learner a picture to draw before the excircle theorem.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.location: OF THE AREA OF A TRIANGLE AND OF THE INSCRIBED CIRCLE
excerpts.latex: This word is often spelled ``\emph{escribed}'' improperly.
excerpts.markdown: This word is often spelled “*escribed*” improperly.
excerpts.why: A short aside on spelling that rewards a curious reader and explains why the word looks odd.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.location: OF THE AREA OF A TRIANGLE AND OF THE INSCRIBED CIRCLE
excerpts.latex: This most useful proposition was known to the Greeks of Alexandria, and by them communicated to the Arabians
excerpts.markdown: This most useful proposition was known to the Greeks of Alexandria, and by them communicated to the Arabians
excerpts.why: Places the mean-proportional result in history, showing that a formula taught today has a long lineage.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.location: OF THE AREA OF A TRIANGLE AND OF THE INSCRIBED CIRCLE
excerpts.latex: whence the area can be calculated in square units when the lengths of the sides are given numerically in units.
excerpts.markdown: whence the area can be calculated in square units when the lengths of the sides are given numerically in units.
excerpts.why: Tells the learner the practical purpose of the result: finding a triangle's area from its three side lengths.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.location: OF THE AREA OF A TRIANGLE AND OF THE INSCRIBED CIRCLE
excerpts.latex: \text{Then, numerically, the Area} = rs.
excerpts.markdown: Then, numerically, the Area = rs.
excerpts.why: Gives the compact numerical form of the area, linking the geometric statement to the symbols s and r a learner will compute with.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: In Euclid an angle is not defined as a magnitude but as the inclination of two lines, which never exceeds two right angles: and in most of the propositions in Euclid it is not necessary to treat an angle otherwise than as a change of direction of a line.
excerpts.markdown: In Euclid an angle is not defined as a magnitude but as the inclination of two lines, which never exceeds two right angles: and in most of the propositions in Euclid it is not necessary to treat an angle otherwise than as a change of direction of a line.
excerpts.why: It shows that the modern wide meaning of angle is a deliberate extension of Euclid's narrower definition, which helps a learner see why the word changes sense.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: So also in Trigonometry, where angular magnitude in general is treated numerically, it is desirable to use the term angle for the sum of a number of angles, which may be greater than two or than any number of right angles.
excerpts.markdown: So also in Trigonometry, where angular magnitude in general is treated numerically, it is desirable to use the term angle for the sum of a number of angles, which may be greater than two or than any number of right angles.
excerpts.why: It explains in plain words why a trigonometric angle may exceed a full turn, which is the idea learners most often find surprising.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: For instance, if a distance $a$~miles be measured from a fixed point~$O$ along (or parallel to) a given line in a standard direction, say east, to~$A$; and a line~$AB$ be cut off from~$OA$ by measuring from~$A$ in the opposite direction, or westward, a distance $b$~miles, the distance~$OB$ may be said to be $= (a - b)$ miles east of~$O$ not only in the case where $a > b$, but also when $a < b$, if it be agreed to interpret the result as meaning $a - b$ east of~$O$ (or in the standard direction) if $a - b$ is a $+$~number, and $b - a$ miles west of~$O$ (or in the contrary direction), when $a - b$ is a $-$~number.
excerpts.markdown: For instance, if a distance $a$ miles be measured from a fixed point $O$ along (or parallel to) a given line in a standard direction, say east, to $A$; and a line $AB$ be cut off from $OA$ by measuring from $A$ in the opposite direction, or westward, a distance $b$ miles, the distance $OB$ may be said to be $= (a - b)$ miles east of $O$ not only in the case where $a > b$, but also when $a < b$, if it be agreed to interpret the result as meaning $a - b$ east of $O$ (or in the standard direction) if $a - b$ is a $+$ number, and $b - a$ miles west of $O$ (or in the contrary direction), when $a - b$ is a $-$ number.
excerpts.why: A worked distance example that shows how a signed result such as a minus b keeps one formula valid whichever quantity is larger.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: Then the standard direction may be called the~$+$ (or positive) direction, and the contrary direction the~$-$ (or negative) direction.
excerpts.markdown: Then the standard direction may be called the $+$ (or positive) direction, and the contrary direction the $-$ (or negative) direction.
excerpts.why: It gives the plain naming of the two directions that a learner needs before any sign convention can be used.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: Again, with reference to angles, if the hand of a going clock be put back through an angle~$\theta$, then, after the time during which the hand moves through an angle~$\phi$, the hand will make an angle $\theta - \phi$ with its present position, the angle being~$+$ and measured in the opposite way to that in which the hand of the clock moves, if $\theta > \phi$; or $-$~and measured in the contrary direction, if $\theta < \phi$.
excerpts.markdown: Again, with reference to angles, if the hand of a going clock be put back through an angle $\theta$, then, after the time during which the hand moves through an angle $\phi$, the hand will make an angle $\theta - \phi$ with its present position, the angle being $+$ and measured in the opposite way to that in which the hand of the clock moves, if $\theta > \phi$; or $-$ and measured in the contrary direction, if $\theta < \phi$.
excerpts.why: A clock-hand picture makes a signed angle concrete and shows that the sign depends on which way the hand has turned.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: In what follows, an angle will be considered as if produced by the revolution of a radius of a circle, the direction of revolution from an initiatory position being considered as $-$~or~$+$ according as it takes place in the direction of the motion of the hand of a clock or the reverse.
excerpts.markdown: In what follows, an angle will be considered as if produced by the revolution of a radius of a circle, the direction of revolution from an initiatory position being considered as $-$ or $+$ according as it takes place in the direction of the motion of the hand of a clock or the reverse.
excerpts.why: It fixes the rotational meaning of angle used for the rest of the chapter, so learners know how the sign of a turn is chosen.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.location: OF THE UNIT OF ANGULAR MAGNITUDE
excerpts.latex: The angle of easiest construction is the angle of an equilateral triangle, which is also two-thirds of a right angle.
excerpts.markdown: The angle of easiest construction is the angle of an equilateral triangle, which is also two-thirds of a right angle.
excerpts.why: It gives learners a concrete angle to picture before any numerical scale is introduced.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.location: OF THE UNIT OF ANGULAR MAGNITUDE
excerpts.latex: It is called the \emph{unit of circular measure}, and the ratio of any angle to this unit is called the \emph{circular measure} of the angle.
excerpts.markdown: It is called the *unit of circular measure*, and the ratio of any angle to this unit is called the *circular measure* of the angle.
excerpts.why: It states plainly that angles can be measured as a ratio to a fixed standard angle, which is the core idea of the chapter.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.location: OF THE UNIT OF ANGULAR MAGNITUDE
excerpts.latex: For such reasons perhaps the sexagesimal scale, which has prevailed since the time of Ptolemy\footnotemark, was originally adopted.
excerpts.markdown: For such reasons perhaps the sexagesimal scale, which has prevailed since the time of Ptolemy, was originally adopted.
excerpts.why: It places the 60-part degree scale in its historical setting and shows that the chapter's conventions have a long history.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.location: OF THE UNIT OF ANGULAR MAGNITUDE
excerpts.latex: Two angles are said to be complements, each of the other, when their sum is a right angle.
excerpts.markdown: Two angles are said to be complements, each of the other, when their sum is a right angle.
excerpts.why: It gives the defining condition for complementary angles in a form learners can test with any pair of angles.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.location: OF THE UNIT OF ANGULAR MAGNITUDE
excerpts.latex: The $60$th part of a degree is a minute, denoted by~$1'$, $\therefore 1° = 60'$.
excerpts.markdown: The $60$th part of a degree is a minute, denoted by $1'$, $\therefore 1° = 60'$.
excerpts.why: It shows the subdivision rule that links minutes to degrees, which learners need before working with angles given in degrees, minutes and seconds.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: When one magnitude or ratio is so connected with another that the former changes with the latter, but is determinable for any given value of the latter, the former is said to be a function of the latter.
excerpts.markdown: When one magnitude or ratio is so connected with another that the former changes with the latter, but is determinable for any given value of the latter, the former is said to be a function of the latter.
excerpts.why: Gives the learner the general idea of a function before any trigonometric ratio appears.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: The side of the hexagon inscribed is $= R$, and it subtends $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ or~$60°$.
excerpts.markdown: The side of the hexagon inscribed is $= R$, and it subtends $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ or $60°$.
excerpts.why: Shows how a known side of an inscribed regular polygon fixes a sine value, the method the chapter uses throughout.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: It should be observed that, while the number~$\theta$ continuously increases, the numbers $\sin\theta$, $\cos\theta$ pass through a series of values between $+1$~and~$-1$, and return to the same values again for every increase of~$2\pi$ in the value of~$\theta$.
excerpts.markdown: It should be observed that, while the number $\theta$ continuously increases, the numbers $\sin\theta$, $\cos\theta$ pass through a series of values between $+1$ and $-1$, and return to the same values again for every increase of $2\pi$ in the value of $\theta$.
excerpts.why: Explains periodicity in plain terms, so the learner sees why angles beyond 2π reuse values.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: If $AF$ be measured towards~$T$, it is to be considered~$+$, and $-$,~if in the contrary direction towards~$T'$.
excerpts.markdown: If $AF$ be measured towards $T$, it is to be considered $+$, and $-$, if in the contrary direction towards $T'$.
excerpts.why: Warns that a tangent's sign depends on the direction it is measured, a common source of sign errors.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: Since the perpendicular from the centre of a circle on any chord bisects it at right angles, the ratio of the chord to the radius is twice the sine of half the angle subtended by the chord.
excerpts.markdown: Since the perpendicular from the centre of a circle on any chord bisects it at right angles, the ratio of the chord to the radius is twice the sine of half the angle subtended by the chord.
excerpts.why: Connects chords and sines in one clear step, and the reason is stated.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: The seven ratios defined above are altogether independent of the size of the circle described, and depend only on the angle.
excerpts.markdown: The seven ratios defined above are altogether independent of the size of the circle described, and depend only on the angle.
excerpts.why: Tells the learner that a circular function is a property of the angle alone, which is the point of the definition.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: From these equations all the functions can be found, when one has been given.
excerpts.markdown: From these equations all the functions can be found, when one has been given.
excerpts.why: Shows that the identities let every circular function be recovered from any one of them.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: But the inventor of Logarithms was not a Peer, and should not be styled Baron Napier as is often done.
excerpts.markdown: But the inventor of Logarithms was not a Peer, and should not be styled Baron Napier as is often done.
excerpts.why: A short historical correction that gives the learner a human story about who invented logarithms and why his title is misremembered.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: Logarithms of ordinary numbers may be defined to be numbers, so calculated from the ordinary numbers, that the sum of the logarithms of two numbers is the logarithm of their product.
excerpts.markdown: Logarithms of ordinary numbers may be defined to be numbers, so calculated from the ordinary numbers, that the sum of the logarithms of two numbers is the logarithm of their product.
excerpts.why: Gives the defining property from which every other logarithm rule follows, so a learner sees why logarithms turn multiplication into addition.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: Thus, with tables, the result of multiplication is calculated by adding logarithms, of division by subtracting logarithms, of raising to a power by multiplying a logarithm by a number, of extracting a root by dividing a logarithm by a number.
excerpts.markdown: Thus, with tables, the result of multiplication is calculated by adding logarithms, of division by subtracting logarithms, of raising to a power by multiplying a logarithm by a number, of extracting a root by dividing a logarithm by a number.
excerpts.why: Summarises in one sentence the four arithmetic operations that the tables turn into simpler ones, which is the practical point of the chapter.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: Equation~\Eq{5} shews that the logarithm increases with the number: therefore it appears that the common logarithm of a number of one integral digit is a proper fraction; that of a number of $2$~digits is $1 + \text{a fraction}$; of $3$~digits $2 + \text{a fraction}$, and so on.
excerpts.markdown: Equation (5) shews that the logarithm increases with the number: therefore it appears that the common logarithm of a number of one integral digit is a proper fraction; that of a number of $2$ digits is $1 + \text{a fraction}$; of $3$ digits $2 + \text{a fraction}$, and so on.
excerpts.why: Shows through the number of digits why the integer part of a common logarithm is what it is, a useful check a learner can apply by hand.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: To avoid the use of negative numbers, the tabular logarithms of the circular functions are the common logarithms of these ratios increased by~$10$: which must be remembered in using the tables in calculations.
excerpts.markdown: To avoid the use of negative numbers, the tabular logarithms of the circular functions are the common logarithms of these ratios increased by $10$: which must be remembered in using the tables in calculations.
excerpts.why: Warns the learner that the printed values of trigonometric logarithms carry an offset of 10, a common source of error when using the tables.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: \First{A triangle} is said to be solved when the sides and angles are calculated from the data.
excerpts.markdown: A triangle is said to be solved when the sides and angles are calculated from the data.
excerpts.why: It states plainly what it means to solve a triangle, which frames every case that follows.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: Then if the side $AB$ be taken as radius, the ratio of $BC$ to $AB$ is the sine of~$A$; and of $AC$ to $AB$ is its cosine;
excerpts.markdown: Then if the side $AB$ be taken as radius, the ratio of $BC$ to $AB$ is the sine of $A$; and of $AC$ to $AB$ is its cosine;
excerpts.why: It defines sine and cosine as ratios of sides in a right-angled triangle, the basis for the right-angle formulas.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex:
or \emph{the sides are proportional to the sines of the opposite angles}.
This is true of all triangles.
excerpts.markdown: or *the sides are proportional to the sines of the opposite angles*. This is true of all triangles.
excerpts.why: It gives the law of sines in words, showing learners why the ratio of each side to the sine of its opposite angle is constant.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: There will always be this ambiguity in determining the angle of a triangle from its sine, unless there be something to point out whether the angle is acute or obtuse: and therefore it is generally inconvenient to use a method involving the determination of the angle from its sine.
excerpts.markdown: There will always be this ambiguity in determining the angle of a triangle from its sine, unless there be something to point out whether the angle is acute or obtuse: and therefore it is generally inconvenient to use a method involving the determination of the angle from its sine.
excerpts.why: It warns that a sine alone does not fix an angle, since the sine of an angle and of its supplement are equal.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: These relations give the simplest logarithmic solution of a triangle, when two sides and the contained angle are given
excerpts.markdown: These relations give the simplest logarithmic solution of a triangle, when two sides and the contained angle are given
excerpts.why: It names the method for two sides and the included angle as the simplest logarithmic route, showing learners how to choose a method.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex:
The formulæ used here were discovered by William Purser of Dublin,
in \Date{1632}.
excerpts.markdown: The formulæ used here were discovered by William Purser of Dublin, in 1632.
excerpts.why: It credits the formulas for solving a triangle from its three sides to a named originator, giving the method a history.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: There is also a simple verification of the process afforded by taking the sum of the three angles, which ought to be~$180°$
excerpts.markdown: There is also a simple verification of the process afforded by taking the sum of the three angles, which ought to be $180°$
excerpts.why: It gives learners a self-check for their answers: the three angles must total 180 degrees.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: In Geodesy, or the application of this part of Trigonometry to surveying, a line, called \emph{the Base}, is measured between two convenient stations; and the angles between lines from these stations to points visible from the stations are measured with appropriate instruments.
excerpts.markdown: In Geodesy, or the application of this part of Trigonometry to surveying, a line, called *the Base*, is measured between two convenient stations; and the angles between lines from these stations to points visible from the stations are measured with appropriate instruments.
excerpts.why: It states the whole method of a trigonometrical survey in one sentence: measure a base, then measure angles from its ends.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: The horizontal angle between two objects is the angle between the vertical planes through the station and each object: it is also called the angle in azimuth.
excerpts.markdown: The horizontal angle between two objects is the angle between the vertical planes through the station and each object: it is also called the angle in azimuth.
excerpts.why: It separates the horizontal angle from the other angle classes, which is the first thing a learner must keep straight in surveying.

excerpts.edition: Macmillan, 1863 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: If the angle of elevation of $C$ be likewise measured at either station, the height of~$C$ above that station can be found by solving a right-angled triangle of which the hypotenuse and one of the acute angles are known.
excerpts.markdown: If the angle of elevation of $C$ be likewise measured at either station, the height of $C$ above that station can be found by solving a right-angled triangle of which the hypotenuse and one of the acute angles are known.
excerpts.why: It shows how a single measured angle of elevation and a right-angled triangle give a height that cannot be reached directly.

excerpts.latex: For details of the measurement of a base, and a description of the instruments principally employed in practical surveying, the reader is referred to Professor Rankine's \textit{Manual of Civil Engineering}, Part~\osf{1}.

excerpts.markdown: Where the extent of the earth’s surface surveyed is too great for the above supposition, the calculations have to be corrected for the sphericity of the earth (see books on Spherical Trigonometry), and in very great and very accurate surveys also for the earth’s deviation from a perfect sphere.
excerpts.why: It warns that flat-earth surveying breaks down over large areas, a limit a learner should know before trusting plane formulas.

excerpts.latex: \First{The} point where the perpendicular from a given point on a given plane or a given line meets the plane or line is called the projection (or more precisely the orthogonal projection) of the point on the plane or line.
excerpts.markdown: The point where the perpendicular from a given point on a given plane or a given line meets the plane or line is called the projection (or more precisely the orthogonal projection) of the point on the plane or line.
excerpts.why: Gives the learner the precise definition of a projection as the foot of a perpendicular.

excerpts.markdown: It is convenient to take one direction of the line of projection (say from left to right) as the $+$ direction and the opposite as the $-$ direction;
excerpts.why: Shows the sign convention that lets a projection carry a sign, which the later proofs depend on.

excerpts.latex: If $BAC$ be acute, $\cos BAC$ is~$+$, and $A'B'$ is~$+$ and is measured from~$A'$ in the $+$~direction; but if $BAC$ be obtuse, $\cos BAC$ is~$-$, and $A'B'$ is~$-$ and is measured from~$A'$ in the $-$~direction.
excerpts.markdown: If $BAC$ be acute, $\cos BAC$ is $+$, and $A'B'$ is $+$ and is measured from $A'$ in the $+$ direction; but if $BAC$ be obtuse, $\cos BAC$ is $-$, and $A'B'$ is $-$ and is measured from $A'$ in the $-$ direction.
excerpts.why: Explains why the sign of the cosine decides the direction of a projection, which is the point learners most often get wrong.

excerpts.markdown: The projection of a broken line is the algebraic sum of the projections of the parts of which it is made up.
excerpts.why: States in one sentence why projections of pieces can be added with their signs, a result that simplifies many problems.
